text:
The Directorate General of Maritime Administration and the Institute of Marine Engineers (India) have signed an Institutional Support Agreement aimed at strengthening India’s engagement at the International Maritime Organization on maritime decarbonisation and sustainability.

What does the Institutional Support Agreement cover?

The collaboration will provide technical, legal and analytical support for India’s submissions and interventions at IMO forums, with particular focus on maritime decarbonisation, alternative fuels, greenhouse gas reduction measures and lifecycle assessment. The partnership will also facilitate stakeholder coordination to support evidence-based policymaking on issues taken up at the Marine Environment Protection Committee and related IMO sub-committees.

Why does this partnership matter for India’s IMO engagement?

By establishing a dedicated institutional support unit, DGMA aims to strengthen the technical depth and consistency of India’s positions at MEPC and IMO sub-committee discussions, ensuring the country’s interventions are backed by rigorous analysis as global shipping regulations around decarbonisation and alternative fuels continue to evolve.

What does this mean for India’s maritime energy transition?

The agreement marks another step in advancing India’s maritime energy transition strategy, reinforcing the country’s role in shaping the global sustainable shipping agenda at a time when IMO member states are actively negotiating greenhouse gas reduction frameworks and alternative fuel pathways for international shipping.

text:
The Philippines has retained its place on the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW) “White List,” reaffirming the country’s compliance with global standards for maritime education and training.

The IMO, a specialized agency of the United Nations that regulates international shipping, maintains the STCW White List of countries that fully comply with the convention’s standards on the education, training, certification and competence of seafarers.

Being on the White List allows certificates issued by the Philippines to be recognized by other IMO member-states, enabling Filipino seafarers to work aboard foreign-going vessels without facing additional certification requirements.

The status also reinforces the country’s standing as one of the world’s leading suppliers of maritime professionals.

The recognition comes after months of heightened risks for thousands of Filipino seafarers deployed in the Middle East.

Amid the US-Iran conflict, the government is closely monitoring Filipino crews transiting the Strait of Hormuz and coordinated with shipping companies and foreign governments to ensure their safety.

The Department of Migrant Workers also extended legal and welfare assistance to the family of a Filipino seafarer involved in a maritime incident in the Strait of Hormuz, while maintaining close coordination with manning agencies amid continuing security concerns in the Persian Gulf.

The recognition confirms that the Philippines continues to meet international requirements for the education, training, assessment, certification and oversight of Filipino seafarers under the STCW Convention.

Maritime Industry Authority Administrator Sonia B. Malaluan welcomed the development, saying the country’s continued inclusion on the White List reflects the strength of the Philippine maritime education and training system.

text:
Kingdom adopts MARPOL Annex VI to reduce ship emissions and protect marine environment

TDT | Manama

Email: mail@newsofbahrain.com

Bahrain has officially joined Annex VI of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), strengthening its commitment to protecting the marine environment and reducing air pollution from the maritime transport sector.

The move brings Bahrain in line with international environmental standards set by the International Maritime Organization (IMO), focusing on controlling harmful emissions from ships and promoting cleaner maritime operations.

MARPOL Annex VI introduces regulations to limit air pollution from vessels, including restrictions on sulfur content in ship fuel, controls on nitrogen oxide emissions from marine engines, and measures to reduce particulate matter and other harmful substances.

The annex also requires ships to obtain the International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate (IAPP) and comply with energy efficiency measures aimed at lowering carbon emissions.

Bahrain had previously joined the MARPOL Convention and its Annexes I, II and V under Law No. (32) of 2005. The accession to Annex VI further expands the Kingdom’s environmental commitments in the maritime sector.

Undersecretary for Ports and Maritime Affairs at the Ministry of Transportation and Telecommunications, Bader Hood Al-Mahmoud, said the move reflects Bahrain’s dedication to supporting global efforts to protect marine ecosystems and reduce emissions from shipping.

He added that Bahrain will continue enhancing maritime inspections and monitoring systems to ensure ships visiting Bahraini ports and vessels registered under the national flag comply with the new environmental requirements.

The implementation of Annex VI is expected to improve the efficiency and sustainability of Bahrain’s maritime sector while reinforcing the Kingdom’s role as a regional maritime hub committed to international environmental standards.

text:
The Kingdom of Bahrain acceded to Annex VI of the 1973 International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), as modified by the 1978 Protocol, reported BNA.

MARPOL aims to protect the environment from pollution and other impacts resulting from shipping operations and maritime navigation through international cooperation among its member states. Its annexes, adopted over time following the convention's entry into force, set out detailed regulations covering different environmental aspects of shipping and maritime activities.

On the accession, Bahraini authorities said it reflects the kingdom's commitment to protecting the marine environment, preserving air quality and reducing emissions from the maritime transport sector in line with international standards and best practices.

It builds on Bahrain's international environmental commitments following its accession to MARPOL and Annexes I, II and V under Law No. (32) of 2005. Annex VI is one of the convention's key environmental annexes, establishing a comprehensive framework to regulate air emissions from ships by setting limits on the sulphur content of marine fuel, regulating nitrogen oxide emissions from ship engines, reducing particulate matter, volatile organic compounds from oil tankers and ozone-depleting substances, stated the report.

It also requires ships to obtain the International Air Pollution Prevention (IAPP) Certificate and comply with energy efficiency and carbon intensity reduction requirements, it added.

Bader Hood Al Mahmood, Undersecretary for Ports and Maritime Affairs at the Ministry of Transportation and Telecommunications, said Bahrain's accession to MARPOL Annex VI reflects the Kingdom's steadfast commitment to supporting international efforts to protect the marine environment and reduce emissions from the maritime transport sector.

"The step demonstrates Bahrain's commitment to keeping pace with developments by adopting the latest standards approved by the International Maritime Organization (IMO), while strengthening the role of maritime navigation in supporting sustainable development and mitigating pollution associated with the sector," he stated.

Al Mahmood said the Ports Affairs will continue to strengthen maritime inspection and oversight systems and ensure implementation of the new environmental requirements for ships visiting Bahraini ports and vessels registered under the Bahraini flag.

These efforts will enhance the efficiency of the maritime sector, support the transition to more sustainable operations and reinforce Bahrain's position as a maritime hub committed to the highest international standards, he added.

Amna Hamad Al Rumaihi, Chief Executive of the Supreme Council for Environment (SCE), said Bahrain's accession to MARPOL Annex VI represents a key milestone in strengthening integrated environmental action and enhancing the Kingdom's contribution to international efforts to protect air quality.

"The move will strengthen inspections of ships visiting Bahraini ports by verifying compliance with fuel and emissions requirements in accordance with IMO standards, while also enhancing compliance by Bahraini-flagged vessels with international environmental requirements, including obtaining the necessary certificates and implementing energy efficiency management plans," she stated.

These measures will help protect the environment and its resources and ensure their sustainability for future generations, she added.

영국 선박기술기업 BAR 테크놀로지스(BAR Technologies)는 EY 그리스(EY Greece)의 해운 탈탄소 보고서에 대한 논평을 통해 "미래 연료 공급 확대나 국제해사기구(IMO)의 넷제로 제도 정착을 기다릴 필요는 없다"며 "정책의 불확실성을 아무것도 하지 않는 이유로 삼아서는 안 된다"고 밝혔다.

EY는 보고서에서 대체연료 공급 부족과 인프라 미비, 조선소 건조 능력, 금융 접근성 등의 제약으로 해운업의 넷제로 전환이 점진적으로 이뤄질 것으로 전망했다. BAR는 이러한 분석에 공감하면서도 에너지 효율 향상과 풍력추진 같은 검증된 기술은 지금 즉시 활용할 수 있는 현실적인 해법이라고 강조했다.

국제풍력선박협회(IWSA)에 따르면 현재 전 세계 100척 이상(500만DWT 이상)의 상선이 풍력추진 시스템을 장착해 운항 중으로, 2022년 5월보다 약 5배 증가했다. BAR도 올해 말까지 WindWings®를 장착한 선박 10척이 운항에 들어가 하루 약 100톤의 이산화탄소(CO₂)를 감축할 것으로 예상했다.

BAR는 풍력추진 확산의 가장 큰 장애물로 상업 구조와 금융 환경을 꼽았다. 현재는 설비 투자 비용은 선주가 부담하지만 연료 절감 효과는 용선자가 가져가는 구조여서 투자 유인이 낮고, 녹색금융 부족으로 자금 조달 비용도 높다는 것이다. 특히 벌크선과 탱커 등 부정기선 시장에서 이러한 문제가 더욱 두드러진다고 설명했다.

존 쿠퍼 BAR 테크놀로지스 CEO는 "풍력추진은 별도의 연료 생산시설이나 벙커링 인프라 구축 없이 즉시 적용할 수 있는 검증된 기술"이라며 "이제 필요한 것은 저금리 녹색금융과 혼합금융, 그리고 연료 절감 효과를 선주와 용선자가 합리적으로 공유할 수 있는 새로운 용선계약 체계"라고 말했다.

text:
The European Commission is facing calls to remove two Indian shipbreaking facilities from its proposed updated list of approved ship recycling yards after an environmental group warned their inclusion would weaken the European Union’s ship recycling standards.

The NGO Shipbreaking Platform said the Commission’s proposal to add Shree Ram and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat, India, to the 16th update of the EU List of ship recycling facilities marks a major change from previous editions of the list.

The Commission has opened a public consultation on the proposed update. It also plans to remove another Turkish shipbreaking yard from the list because of recurring deficiencies.

According to the NGO, approving the two beaching yards would raise concerns about the future direction of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation (EU SRR), which is intended to ensure ships are recycled safely and in an environmentally sound way.

The group said that if the Commission’s assessment allows facilities that pose risks to coastal ecosystems, workers and nearby communities to be approved, the regulation’s objectives would not be achieved.

Beaching, the main method used for shipbreaking in South Asia, involves dismantling ships directly on tidal mudflats without infrastructure to contain pollution.

The NGO said this allows debris and hazardous materials, including oil, fuel and liquid chemical residues, to enter seawater and contribute to environmental damage.

“None of the beaching yards would be allowed to clone their operations on a tidal mudflat in the EU. Their inclusion on the EU List will set a chilling double standard and seriously undermine the EU’s own ship recycling sector,” said Ingvild Jenssen, Executive Director and Founder of NGO Shipbreaking Platform.

The organisation also referred to a heavy fuel spill at the Priya Blue shipbreaking yard in June 2026. It said the spill contaminated large areas of the Gujarat coast and was visible up to 10 kilometres from the yard.

Although the yard said it responded immediately, the NGO argued the incident showed the difficulty of containing pollutants when ships are dismantled on tidal mudflats.

The group also said these operations violate coastal regulation zone boundaries. While Indian courts have generally favoured regulating the practice rather than banning it, environmental groups believe the current framework is not enough to ensure safe and environmentally sound ship recycling because of the environmental and occupational health risks associated with beaching.

The NGO also pointed to the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, which the European Union and its member states have signed. End-of-life ships are covered under the convention as hazardous waste.

It said the convention aims to prevent hazardous waste from being exported to countries that do not have the capacity to manage it safely. The Basel Ban Amendment also prohibits the movement of hazardous waste from OECD countries to non-OECD countries.

“While the EU has a responsibility to ensure that it does not export harm to third countries, the standards of the EU SRR cannot change based on the location. Every yard on the EU List should be subject to the same rules and procedures. If not, compliant yards in the EU will continue to face unfair competition,” Jenssen said.

She urged the European Commission to reject practices that would not be allowed within the European Union and to prevent the shipping industry from taking advantage of weaker environmental and occupational health and safety standards.

The European Commission’s public consultation on the proposed 16th update of the EU List of ship recycling facilities is ongoing, and the proposed inclusion of the two Indian yards will be considered before a final decision is made.

text:
CEBU CITY—Measures to modernize the Maritime Industry Authority (Marina), amend the Domestic Shipping Development Act, strengthen the Coast Guard (PCG), and streamline maritime regulations topped the agenda of the Philippine Coastwise Shipping Association Inc. (PCSA) as lawmakers pledged to push policy reforms and increased government support for the domestic shipping industry.

During the PCSA General Membership Meeting in Cebu City on Friday, Quezon City Rep. Franz Pumaren, chairman of the House Committee on Transportation, assured shipping stakeholders that Congress is pursuing a package of reforms aimed at improving maritime safety while reducing operational bottlenecks that have long burdened domestic ship operators.

Among the priority measures under deliberation are bills strengthening the PCG’s safety and environmental protection functions, creating an independent National Transportation Safety Board, amending Republic Act 9295 or the Domestic Shipping Development Act of 2004, reforming the country’s pilotage system, modernizing Marina through digitalization, improving

the Philippine ship registry, and implementing broader maritime safety reforms, including stricter seaworthiness audits and mandatory cargo weighing.

Pumaren said the proposed measures seek to strike a balance between ensuring passenger safety and maintaining a competitive domestic shipping sector.

“We will push for reforms that protect passengers, crew, cargo and communities while modernizing government agencies without creating unnecessary bureaucracy,” he said.

The legislative agenda came in response to concerns raised by PCSA Chairman Lucio Lim, who urged Congress to champion reforms that would ease regulatory burdens and improve government support for the shipping industry.

Foremost among these is addressing Marina’s manpower shortage, which Lim said has resulted in delays in vessel inspections, certification and document processing despite ships already being ready for departure.

Lim said Marina had around 1,100 personnel in 2016, and only about 1,200 employees today despite the agency’s expanded responsibilities.

Of its workforce, roughly 40 percent are job-order employees, while only 152 serve as inspectors and surveyors overseeing an estimated fleet of 24,000 vessels.

He added that the situation could become more challenging as Marina assumes additional responsibilities over maritime higher education under recent legislation.

In response, Pumaren said Congress would study increasing Marina’s budget during the upcoming budget deliberations to help address staffing deficiencies and improve inspection capabilities.

“We will look at how we can increase funding for Marina so that inspection delays and manpower shortages can be addressed,” he said.

However, former President and PCSA Chairperson Emeritus Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo said automation offers a more practical long-term solution than expanding the bureaucracy.

She noted that automating clerical functions would allow Marina to deploy more personnel to inspection work while making government services more efficient.

Pumaren agreed, saying digital transformation forms part of the committee’s proposed reforms for Marina, particularly in vessel registration, crew certification, compliance monitoring and maritime safety systems.

Beyond Marina, Lim also appealed for a review of the implementation of international maritime conventions, arguing that regulations intended for international vessels are being applied to domestic shipping, driving up operating costs.

He, likewise, called on the Philippine Ports Authority (PPA) to provide broader fee relief similar to the measures adopted by the Cebu Port Authority, which temporarily waived passenger terminal, berthing and roll-on/roll-off (RoRo) terminal fees.

Lim said these charges account for only a small portion of the PPA’s revenues but significantly increase transport costs, particularly for inter-island shipping serving the Visayas and Mindanao.

The PCSA chairman also urged the Coast Guard to reconsider its policy requiring physical clearance for every vessel departure, saying the practice causes operational delays and creates opportunities for corruption.

He said the association has already raised the matter with PCG officials, who are considering initially applying alternative clearance procedures for cargo vessels.

Lim also pressed for renewed government attention to the Strong Republic Nautical Highway network, citing deteriorating road links to several ports over the past five years.

He noted that RoRo services have become a vital logistics backbone for e-commerce and cargo movement, allowing goods to reach Cebu, Bacolod, Iloilo and Tacloban within two days and Mindanao destinations such as Cagayan de Oro and Davao in about three days.

Pumaren, for his part, emphasized that Congress views industry stakeholders as partners in crafting practical legislation.

“Good legislation cannot be crafted inside committee rooms alone. It must be informed by the operational realities you face every day,” he told PCSA members.

The committee, he added, remains committed to develop policies that improve maritime safety while supporting investment, operational efficiency and long-term growth in the country’s domestic shipping industry.

Ferry Hull 096, dubbed China Zorrilla after the Uruguayan actor, was completed in May 2025 by Hobart ship builder Incat.

It can transport up to 2100 passengers and more than 200 vehicles and will service a route between Uruguay and Argentina.

Electric ferry Hull 096 has been loaded onto heavy lift vessel Black Marlin in the River Derwent. (PR IMAGE PHOTO)

On Friday, it was successfully loaded aboard the 217m-long and 42m-wide heavy-lift ship Black Marlin in Hobart's River Derwent.

The operation, in which the Black Marlin became semi-submerged for Hull 096 to move onto its deck, was dubbed one of the most complex in Tasmania's maritime history.

"This is an extraordinary moment, not just for Incat but for the future of sustainable maritime transport," Incat chairman Robert Clifford said.

"For years we've watched this vessel evolve from an idea into reality, and today we've reached another incredible milestone in the most significant project in Incat's history."

The 130m-long Incat electric ferry carries a 40-megawatt energy storage system. (PR IMAGE PHOTO)

Hull 096, which is 130m long, features the largest retail shopping space on any ferry, spanning 2300sq m.

It carries a 40-megawatt energy storage system and will charge via ports on each side of the River Pate in South America.

Mr Clifford described the vessel as a trailblazer in the shift to more environmentally friendly ferries and said Incat had more electric vessels in the works.

The Black Marlin had to become semi-submerged for Hull 096 to move onto its deck. (PR IMAGE PHOTO)

"It demonstrates ... the future of high-speed, large-capacity ferry transport is here," he said.

"We are incredibly proud that this technology has been designed and built in Tasmania and that it will soon be operating on one of the world's busiest ferry routes."

text:
Brazil has opened a public consultation on plans to update its marine fuel regulations, proposing changes that would expand the use of biofuels and alternative marine fuels in the country's shipping sector.

The National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) published the draft proposal on July 27 to update Resolution No. 903/2022, which sets specifications for marine diesel oil and marine fuel oil sold in Brazil.

The draft would align Brazil's marine fuel specifications with ISO 8217:2024 and support the sector's energy transition, international law firm Mayer Brown said on its website on Wednesday.

Among the proposed changes is approval for up to B100 (100% marine biofuel) to be supplied for routine use by ships, rather than only under exceptional circumstances.

The regulator also plans to recognise HVO, green diesel and gas-to-liquids (GTL) fuels as drop-in alternatives that can be used without changes to engines or bunkering infrastructure.

The proposal would also replace the current requirement for prior ANP authorisation of biofuel blending with a notification system for authorised blending companies.

Methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and ethanol would still require ANP experimental approval before they can be bunkered, while LNG would move to a separate authorisation process reflecting the availability of established technical standards.

The changes would bring the country's rules more closely into line with international standards and provide a clearer framework for biofuel operations already taking place in its maritime sector.

title: Report Calls for Common Standards for Safe Havens in Ammonia-Fuelled Ships
description:
The shipping industry needs a common approach to designing and assessing emergency safe havens on ammonia-fuelled ships, according to a new report from the Lloyd's Register Maritime Decarbonisation Hub.
A safe haven is a sealed refuge where crew can shelter from toxic ammonia gas during a leak while maintaining control of the vessel or preparing to abandon ship if necessary.
The IMO’s interim guidelines for the safety of ships using ammonia as Fuel require ammonia-fuelled vessels to be fitted with safe havens, but the report argues the guidelines provide only high-level requirements, leaving room for different interpretations.
The report says safe havens should be treated as part of a vessel's wider emergency response system and designed around three core functions: protection, command and control, and accessibility.
It also recommends testing them against standardised worst-case ammonia release scenarios, including major bunkering incidents, and maintaining them throughout a vessel's service life.
text:
The shipping industry needs a common approach to designing and assessing emergency safe havens on ammonia-fuelled ships, according to a new report from the Lloyd's Register Maritime Decarbonisation Hub.

A safe haven is a sealed refuge where crew can shelter from toxic ammonia gas during a leak while maintaining control of the vessel or preparing to abandon ship if necessary.

The IMO’s interim guidelines for the safety of ships using ammonia as Fuel require ammonia-fuelled vessels to be fitted with safe havens, but the report argues the guidelines provide only high-level requirements, leaving room for different interpretations.

It warns this could result in varying levels of safety across the future ammonia-powered fleet and proposes a common assessment framework to help designers, classification societies and flag administrations adopt a more consistent approach.

The recommendations draw on established practices in the offshore oil and gas and chemical industries.

The report says safe havens should be treated as part of a vessel's wider emergency response system and designed around three core functions: protection, command and control, and accessibility.

It also recommends testing them against standardised worst-case ammonia release scenarios, including major bunkering incidents, and maintaining them throughout a vessel's service life.

title: China leads in alternative fuels as Europe loses ground - Seatrade Maritime News
description:
European NGO Transport & Environment (T&E) argues that instability of supply of fossil fuels makes it crucial for Europe to remain competitive in the race to develop alternative fuels.
T&E told Seatrade Maritime News: “Maritime transport is a global sector and green e-fuels will be required globally to decarbonise it.
Shipping in Europe has been slow commit to alternative fuels while the regulatory uncertainty around the EU ETS and global regulations are also delaying investment.
Owners need clearer signals as to the direction of travel for alternative fuels before they can make major investments.
That is not just about the economics of fuel, it is also about the geopolitical tensions created by dependency on strategic energy supply.
text:
European NGO Transport & Environment (T&E) argues that instability of supply of fossil fuels makes it crucial for Europe to remain competitive in the race to develop alternative fuels.

According to the NGO Europe is at risk of losing ground in the race to produce net zero fuels as China, with fewer projects, is producing more fuel as the lack of European offtake agreements is hampering development.

T&E told Seatrade Maritime News: “Maritime transport is a global sector and green e-fuels will be required globally to decarbonise it. China's recent investment confirms the role these fuels will play for decarbonisation.”

In addition, T&E believes the shift to net zero fuels, “Signifies the transition away from the sector's reliance on imported fossil fuels that have become less reliable and [less] stable due to the various crises and conflicts in recent years.”

Commercial viability is critical in the development of e-fuels according to Martin Crawford-Brunt, founder of consultancy Lookout Maritime, who pointed to the profits made by sustainable aviation fuel leader Neste, that has seen a profit spike largely due to the Middle East uncertainty, in the first half of this year.

Neste’s H1 profits were up from €551 million in the first half of last year to €2.06 billion this year.

“Neste shows that there is a business case for e-fuels,” said Crawford-Brunt.

Even so, statistics released today by T&E reveal that Europe has 69 projects planned for alternative fuels, many of them targeting maritime operators, that are projected to produce 4.09 million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe) energy.

By comparison, China has 15 e-fuel projects with an estimated output of 1.72 Mtoe by 2029. But whereas in China three are already operational, a further 10 are under construction and two more are past the final investment decision (FID) stage.

In Europe, of the 69 projects three are operational, one other has confirmed its investment decision, while all 65 other projects have FIDs pending.

“We know that most EU-based projects are struggling to confirm final investment decisions, which in turn often depend on reliable multi-year demand signals,” said a T&E spokesperson.

Shipping in Europe has been slow commit to alternative fuels while the regulatory uncertainty around the EU ETS and global regulations are also delaying investment.

Owners need clearer signals as to the direction of travel for alternative fuels before they can make major investments.

Crawford-Brunt believes that it will take regulatory certainty to drive binding offtake agreements, which he says are largely driven by land-based investment decisions, with maritime and aviation requiring just 10% each of the available energy.

According to T&E that commercial imperative is also laced with a more prosaic security issue.

“Green and alternative fuels are a growing market, Europe should become a clean fuel producer in its own right to supply its bunker hubs, especially as these fuels become an important strategic asset, to avoid dependence on fuels imported via increasingly unstable shipping routes,” said the T&E spokesperson.

That is not just about the economics of fuel, it is also about the geopolitical tensions created by dependency on strategic energy supply.

“It is a question of keeping pace, ensuring supply and investing in future energy sources rather than switching one dependency for another.”

title: Hydrogen-powered shipping could deliver $284 billion in annual health benefits
description:
Global modeling suggests that replacing conventional marine fuels with hydrogen could sharply reduce pollution-related mortality while generating substantial health and economic benefits.
Study: Health and economic impacts of improved air quality from transitioning global shipping energy to hydrogen.
The modeled improvements in air quality translated into substantial estimated health benefits worldwide.
The researchers estimated global monetized health benefits of approximately 284 billion US dollars under the complete transition scenario and 114 billion US dollars under the partial transition scenario.
India was projected to experience the highest economic benefits, followed by Japan, the United States, Italy, and China.
text:
Global modeling suggests that replacing conventional marine fuels with hydrogen could sharply reduce pollution-related mortality while generating substantial health and economic benefits.

Study: Health and economic impacts of improved air quality from transitioning global shipping energy to hydrogen. Image Credit: Audio und werbung / Shutterstock

In a recent study published online as an unedited 'Article in Press' in the journal Nature Communications, a group of researchers estimated the potential global health and economic benefits of replacing conventional shipping fuels with hydrogen using integrated air quality, health, and economic models.

Background

Worldwide maritime operations burn large amounts of fossil fuels and emit significant amounts of pollutants annually, leading to poor air quality and premature deaths. Although new regulations in the shipping industry have limited sulfur and nitrogen oxide emissions, shipping continues to emit substantial amounts of carbon dioxide (CO2), fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and ozone-forming pollutants, particularly in densely populated coastal regions.

Hydrogen has emerged as a potential low-carbon fuel option for the maritime sector. The study assumed that hydrogen-powered vessels would produce negligible air-pollutant emissions during operation, although hydrogen production can generate upstream emissions. The associated air-quality, health, and economic co-benefits remain poorly characterized.

About the Study

The researchers estimated the potential health and economic effects of replacing conventional marine fuels with hydrogen using an integrated modeling framework that combined emissions estimation, atmospheric simulation, health risk assessment, and economic valuation. The framework incorporated the Community Earth System Model version 2.2 (CESM2.2), concentration-response models (CRMs), and the value of statistical life (VSL) approach.

Three principal scenarios were examined, with the baseline representing global shipping emissions and atmospheric conditions in 2022, incorporating existing International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations but assuming no hydrogen adoption.

The next two pathways represented upper-bound and partial scenarios: in the former, hydrogen met all shipping energy demand; in the latter, hydrogen supplied 50% of demand while fossil fuels supplied the remainder. Hydrogen production locations and capacity were based on globally announced low- and zero-emission projects through 2050, with the complete and partial pathways allocating 30% and 15% of projected production to shipping, respectively.

The model simulated changes in global annual mean PM2.5 and maximum daily average 8-hour (MDA8) ozone concentrations after the transition to hydrogen. The air quality estimates were combined with 2019 population data and 2021 baseline mortality rates for adults aged 25 years or older to calculate premature deaths due to pollution using standard exposure-response relationships, including the Global Exposure Mortality Model (GEMM) for PM2.5 and a log-linear ozone concentration model. Subsequently, the monetized value of avoided premature deaths was calculated using country-specific VSL adjusted to 2022 purchasing power parity values.

Study Results

The models projected that transitioning from fossil fuels to hydrogen could substantially reduce global shipping emissions and improve air quality in many coastal and marine areas. Although hydrogen production could increase some land-based emissions associated with fuel generation, emissions from ships were assumed to fall to zero under a complete transition and to half under a partial transition. Global annual emissions of major pollutants, including sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs), and primary organic matter (POM), were projected to decline most under the complete transition scenario.

These emission reductions drove improvements in air quality around the globe as modeled. This produced lower modeled ground-level PM2.5 concentrations around major international shipping routes and various ports, especially in East Asia, Southeast Asia, and some areas of the Mediterranean Sea.

In contrast, localized increases in PM2.5 were projected in a few areas, including parts of the United States Gulf Coast, northern Chile, Western Europe, and northwest India, largely due to emissions from hydrogen production facilities. Similar trends were observed in the partial transition experiment, though with smaller changes.

The largest modeled concentration changes involved MDA8 ozone. Ozone levels were projected to decline by more than 10 parts per billion (ppb) along major shipping corridors and decreased across many coastal regions worldwide. However, limited increases in ozone were projected in a few urban and industrialized locations because lower NO emissions altered local atmospheric chemistry. Even when the researchers assumed an extreme 10% hydrogen leakage rate, the overall spatial pattern and magnitude of ozone improvements remained largely unchanged, indicating that the projected air quality benefits changed little under this assumption.

The modeled improvements in air quality translated into substantial estimated health benefits worldwide. Under the complete hydrogen transition scenario, an estimated 129,458 premature deaths could be prevented each year, while the partial transition scenario was estimated to prevent 52,574 premature deaths annually.

During the complete transition, approximately 75% of the deaths avoided were attributed to reduced ozone exposure, and around 25% to decreased PM2.5 concentrations. Eastern Asia and Southeastern Asia showed the largest PM2.5-attributable benefits, whereas Southern Asia showed the largest ozone-attributable benefits.

While China had the highest estimated reduction in PM2.5-attributable premature deaths, India had the highest estimated reduction in ozone-attributable premature deaths. Certain areas, including eastern China, the western coast of the Korean Peninsula, Singapore, and northwestern coastal Italy, recorded local increases in ozone-attributable mortality as lower NO emissions weakened ozone titration. Some regions also experienced minor increases in PM2.5-attributable mortality associated with hydrogen production.

Avoiding premature mortality also generated substantial monetized health benefits. The researchers estimated global monetized health benefits of approximately 284 billion US dollars under the complete transition scenario and 114 billion US dollars under the partial transition scenario.

India was projected to experience the highest economic benefits, followed by Japan, the United States, Italy, and China. However, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar were projected to have negative monetized health effects because of localized increases in ozone-related mortality, but the global total remained positive.

These figures represent the estimated value of changes in mortality risk, not direct financial savings or a complete assessment of transition costs and benefits.

Conclusion

The findings indicated that replacing conventional shipping fuels with hydrogen could substantially improve global air quality while delivering major public health and monetized economic benefits. The largest reductions in premature mortality were projected to result from lower ozone exposure, with additional gains from decreased PM2.5 concentrations. Health improvements were estimated to be especially pronounced in densely populated regions with high shipping activity, particularly across Asia.

The study also showed that a complete transition to hydrogen was projected to produce considerably greater total benefits than a partial transition and that the projected advantages changed little under the extreme 10% hydrogen-leakage assumption. However, these scenarios were idealized projections rather than forecasts.

The model held shipping patterns and nonshipping emissions constant, neglected hydrogen-transport emissions and climate-change effects, and combined atmospheric, population, mortality, and hydrogen-project inputs from different years.

Hydrogen-powered shipping could play an important role in advancing cleaner maritime transport while supporting global public health and economic welfare, provided that the associated production, infrastructure, cost, and technical challenges are addressed.

title: It is not diesel powering these ships, it is seawater: Britain says a new system turns saltwater ...
description:
It can then be fed to a hydrogen combustion engine instead of diesel.
This is not the first seawater hydrogen test Direct seawater electrolysis is already an active research field.
GH2DEM is presented as Britain’s first all-in-one maritime demonstrator linking direct seawater electrolysis, ambient storage, and a heavy-duty combustion engine.
The exhaust still needs scrutiny Hydrogen combustion eliminates fuel-derived carbon dioxide, but “only steam” is too tidy a description.
It is a full marine trial showing energy use, hydrogen output, storage capacity, engine emissions, durability, and cost under real operating conditions.
text:
A British team has built a land-based demonstrator designed to turn seawater into hydrogen, store it at ordinary temperature and pressure, and use it in a heavy-duty marine engine. Called GH2DEM, the project combines Brunel University of London’s engine research with Genuine H2’s electrolysis and storage technology.

Its first targets are ferries, fishing boats, tugboats, and port vessels that may struggle with the weight, space, or charging needs of large batteries.

Sounds like a ship powered by the sea itself. Not quite. Renewable electricity supplies the energy, while seawater provides the hydrogen, so the real test is whether the full chain can be efficient, durable, safe, and affordable outside the lab.

How the system works

The system draws in salt water and sends it to specialized electrodes that separate hydrogen without a conventional desalination stage. That could reduce the equipment, energy use, and maintenance associated with desalinating water onboard. Professor Xinyan Wang summed up the idea simply when he said, “Water will be turned into power.”

After production, the hydrogen is captured in what the team describes as a molecular solid using a nano-film thinner than paper. It can then be fed to a hydrogen combustion engine instead of diesel. Because the fuel contains no carbon, the engine produces no carbon dioxide from the hydrogen itself.

The storage idea may matter most

Making hydrogen is only half the problem. Packing enough of it onto a vessel without sacrificing cargo space is a long-running obstacle because hydrogen has high energy by weight but low energy by volume. Today’s common options rely on bulky high-pressure tanks or cryogenic systems.

Brunel says GH2DEM’s film holds hydrogen at room temperature and normal pressure, avoiding giant pressure vessels or cryogenic cooling to roughly minus 418°F. In practical terms, that could make the package easier to fit into a crowded engine room. However, the team still has to prove how much hydrogen the material can carry, how quickly it releases the fuel, and how it performs after repeated cycles.

This is not the first seawater hydrogen test

Direct seawater electrolysis is already an active research field. A 2024 study in Nature Communications reported a floating, wind-powered platform that operated for more than 240 hours under changing ocean conditions. The British project’s claimed first is narrower and more useful to understand.

GH2DEM is presented as Britain’s first all-in-one maritime demonstrator linking direct seawater electrolysis, ambient storage, and a heavy-duty combustion engine. That integration is the point. A good electrolyzer on its own does not move a boat, and a good engine is little help without safe fuel storage.

Why shipping is looking for alternatives

Shipping accounted for about 2.89% of global human-caused carbon dioxide emissions in 2018, according to the International Maritime Organization. The IMO’s strategy calls for at least a 20% cut in international shipping emissions by 2030 compared with 2008, while aiming for net zero around 2050. That clock is moving fast for vessels that can remain in service for decades.

For short routes, batteries can work well and remove engine exhaust altogether. Fishing boats, ferries, and tugboats, however, may spend long hours away from a charger, carry heavy loads, or need quick refueling between jobs. Nobody wants a cleaner harbor vessel that cannot finish its shift.

The exhaust still needs scrutiny

Hydrogen combustion eliminates fuel-derived carbon dioxide, but “only steam” is too tidy a description. High-temperature combustion in air can create nitrogen oxides, which harm air quality. Engine tuning, lean operation, and exhaust treatment may therefore be needed.

The climate result also depends on the electricity. If the electrolyzer runs on wind, solar, or another low-carbon source, the hydrogen can be genuinely low-carbon. If it draws heavily from fossil power, emissions are shifted upstream rather than erased.

Salt water is a harsh workplace

Seawater is not gentle on machinery. Chloride can trigger unwanted chlorine reactions and corrode electrodes, while calcium and magnesium deposits can clog surfaces and weaken performance. Waves, vibration, salt spray, and months of continuous operation only make the engineering harder.

That is why a land demonstrator is not the finish line. The system must show stable efficiency, safe hydrogen handling, reliable storage, and predictable engine performance during real voyages. Regulators and ship operators will also want clear evidence before putting it beside crews, cargo, and hot machinery.

Funding and the next milestone

Brunel said GH2DEM received roughly $1.9 million from the Department for Transport’s UK SHORE initiative and Innovate UK, part of a wider clean-maritime push worth about $40 million based on July 22, 2026, exchange rates.

UK research records list the project as running from August 2025 through March 2026. The Centre for Process Innovation was also brought in to help examine manufacturing at scale, while Brunel’s public release described land testing rather than commercial sea deployment.

Where could it work first? The strongest near-term case is likely on coastal and harbor vessels that return to predictable locations, have limited space, and burn a lot of diesel over repeated routes. Big ocean-going ships may require far more fuel and a tougher business case.

The next proof point is not another eye-catching claim about “water-powered” ships. It is a full marine trial showing energy use, hydrogen output, storage capacity, engine emissions, durability, and cost under real operating conditions.

name: International Maritime Organization
title: Sulphur compliance: Expanding ECAs are only as effective as their enforcement
description:
The Mediterranean ECA entered into force in 2025, while the Canadian Arctic and Norwegian Sea ECAs are set to follow in 2027.
As sulphur compliance is still largely verified through retrospective or documentation-based methods, there is often a lag between regulation and assured performance at sea.
Sulphur emissions from shipping contribute to respiratory disease, cardiovascular illness and premature mortality, particularly in densely populated coastal regions.
The challenge is that compliance verification has not evolved at the same pace as regulation.
A larger ECA network inevitably means a larger monitoring challenge and without effective verification tools, regulatory ambition risks outpacing enforcement capability.
text:
The International Maritime Organization’s decision to adopt a new Emission Control Area (ECA) for the North-East Atlantic marks another significant step in the global effort to reduce shipping’s impact on air quality. Covering waters off Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Ireland, the United Kingdom, France, Spain and Portugal, the new ECA will introduce a 0.1% sulphur limit from 2028, further extending one of shipping’s most effective environmental regulations.

The decision from the IMO reflects a wider trend. The Mediterranean ECA entered into force in 2025, while the Canadian Arctic and Norwegian Sea ECAs are set to follow in 2027. Alongside the Baltic Sea, North Sea and North American ECAs, an increasing proportion of the world’s busiest shipping routes and ports now operate under the strictest sulphur controls available.

Yet as the map of regulated waters grows, an important question remains: how effectively are existing limits being enforced?

As sulphur compliance is still largely verified through retrospective or documentation-based methods, there is often a lag between regulation and assured performance at sea. That gap has direct implications beyond policy. Air pollution remains an immediate public health issue. Sulphur emissions from shipping contribute to respiratory disease, cardiovascular illness and premature mortality, particularly in densely populated coastal regions. The impact is felt not only by communities living near ports and shipping lanes, but also by seafarers and port workers who face prolonged exposure to vessel emissions.

This is particularly significant when considering the difference between marine and road fuels. While sulphur content in road fuels across Europe is limited to just 10 parts per million (ppm), marine fuels operating outside ECAs may contain substantially higher concentrations. ECAs were designed to address that disparity, but their effectiveness ultimately depends on compliance.

The challenge is that compliance verification has not evolved at the same pace as regulation.

Across Europe, thousands of vessel inspections continue to rely primarily on documentation, bunker delivery notes and fuel records rather than direct emissions measurement. Physical fuel sampling remains an important enforcement tool, but it is resource-intensive, time-consuming and often provides results only after a vessel has departed. By the time non-compliance is identified, the ship is gone and the damage, to air quality, to public health, to the credibility of the regulation itself, is already done.

This creates a difficult situation for regulators and a frustrating one for responsible ship operators. Shipowners investing in compliant fuels, scrubber technology and emissions management systems expect a level playing field. Where verification is inconsistent, there is a risk that non-compliant operators gain a commercial advantage while avoiding detection.

The issue becomes even more significant as sulphur regulations expand into new regions. A larger ECA network inevitably means a larger monitoring challenge and without effective verification tools, regulatory ambition risks outpacing enforcement capability.

Continuous emissions monitoring systems and real-time digital verification tools are already changing what is possible. Vessels can now be monitored remotely, continuously and without the delays that make retrospective enforcement so limited. Port state control authorities have access to richer data than ever before, the opportunity now is to ensure enforcement frameworks evolve quickly enough to make full use of it.

The significance of this shift to better monitoring extends beyond enforcement alone; it is changing how emissions performance is assessed and trusted across the industry. Charterers, cargo owners, investors and financial institutions are increasingly seeking verified environmental performance data. Demonstrating compliance through continuous monitoring can support ESG reporting, strengthen stakeholder confidence and reduce operational risk.

The expansion of ECAs across Europe and beyond represents a major achievement for international environmental regulation. But achievements on paper are not achievements in practice. The success of these measures will not ultimately be judged by the size of the areas they cover, but by the confidence regulators, industry and the public have that the limits are being enforced.

title: Shipping Must Stop Treating Decarbonisation As A 'Future Fuel' Problem, Says BAR Technologies
description:
BAR Technologies argues that wind propulsion, already delivering measurable fuel and emissions savings on commercial vessels, must be recognised as a proven part of that immediate response.
Wind propulsion has also passed an important market milestone.
John Cooper, CEO of BAR Technologies, said: “Shipping needs to stop treating decarbonisation as something that only begins when future fuels arrive or every detail of the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework is settled.
Without competitive green lending or blended finance, owners may have to fund emissions-reduction technology at conventional commercial borrowing rates.
Shipowners need access to financing that makes proven emissions-reduction technologies commercially viable today, not at some point in the future.
text:
A new study by EY Greece has warned that shipping’s transition to net zero will be uneven and capital intensive, constrained by factors including alternative fuel availability, infrastructure, shipyard capacity, access to finance and fragmented commercial incentives.

Responding to the report, BAR Technologies said that while the industry is right to plan for long-term fuel pathways, too much of the decarbonisation debate remains focused on what may become available in the future rather than what can be deployed now.

The EY study identifies energy efficiency and operational measures as among the most practical near-term actions available to shipping. BAR Technologies argues that wind propulsion, already delivering measurable fuel and emissions savings on commercial vessels, must be recognised as a proven part of that immediate response.

Wind propulsion has also passed an important market milestone. According to the International Windship Association, more than 100 large commercial cargo ships, representing over five million tonnes of deadweight capacity, are now equipped to harness wind power. That is almost five times the number recorded in May 2022, clear evidence that the technology is moving into the commercial mainstream. BAR Technologies are playing a significant part in this transition: By the end of 2026, 10 vessels will be operating with 23 WindWings® installed, giving a combined saving of approximately 100t of CO2 per day.

John Cooper, CEO of BAR Technologies, said: “Shipping needs to stop treating decarbonisation as something that only begins when future fuels arrive or every detail of the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework is settled. The industry cannot allow the absence of perfect policy certainty to become an excuse for inaction. Proven technologies are available now, and owners can act today.”

Unlike alternative fuels, wind requires no new fuel-production facilities, bunkering infrastructure or global supply chain. It is freely available as an energy source and can reduce a vessel’s dependence on whichever fuel it uses.

Cooper continued: “Wind propulsion is not waiting to be invented or proven. It is already operating on commercial vessels and reducing the amount of fuel they need. The priority now should be to remove the barriers preventing more owners from investing.”

For wind propulsion, those barriers are increasingly commercial and financial rather than technical.

Under many chartering arrangements, the owner funds the technology while the charterer receives much of the benefit through lower fuel consumption. Until charterparty structures allow the costs, risks and savings to be shared more effectively, owners can be left carrying the investment and long-term performance risk.

Access to finance is another significant constraint. Without competitive green lending or blended finance, owners may have to fund emissions-reduction technology at conventional commercial borrowing rates. This can lengthen the payback period, particularly in the tramp, bulk and tanker markets, where routes, earnings and charter durations are less predictable.

The EY study concludes that the pace of shipping’s transition will depend on coordination, commercial bankability, access to finance and action across the maritime value chain.

Cooper added: “But the real way to unlock action now is to make green investment affordable. Shipowners need access to financing that makes proven emissions-reduction technologies commercially viable today, not at some point in the future. If we can lower the cost of capital and create funding structures that recognise both the fuel savings and the environmental value these technologies deliver, far more owners will be able to invest.

“Wind propulsion has already passed the technology test. Affordable finance, alongside charterparty structures that share the benefits fairly, is what will unlock deployment at scale.”

title: SAAM Hunabku to be the first tugboat featuring IMO Tier III technology in Guatemala
description:
SAAM Towage will soon add the tug SAAM Hunabku to its fleet, making it the company's 16th vessel delivered by Sanmar Shipyards.
It will operate out of Puerto Quetzal, Guatemala, as part of the company's fleet renewal program in the Americas.
Pablo Cáceres, SAAM Towage’s Manager of Innovation and New Construction, noted that “the SAAM Hunabku will enable more environmentally friendly operations at Puerto Quetzal, as the first IMO Tier III tugboat in Guatemala.
This milestone reaffirms the path we have outlined to advance our sustainability strategy and reflects the valuable partnership we have built with Sanmar to achieve our goals."

SAAM Towage will soon add the tug SAAM Hunabku to its fleet, making it the company's 16th vessel delivered by Sanmar Shipyards. It will operate out of Puerto Quetzal, Guatemala, as part of the company's fleet renewal program in the Americas.

Pablo Cáceres, SAAM Towage’s Manager of Innovation and New Construction, noted that “the SAAM Hunabku will enable more environmentally friendly operations at Puerto Quetzal, as the first IMO Tier III tugboat in Guatemala. This milestone reaffirms the path we have outlined to advance our sustainability strategy and reflects the valuable partnership we have built with Sanmar to achieve our goals."

IMO Tier III classification certifies that the engines meet the highest international standards for nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions control, contributing to more efficient and environmentally friendly operations.

For his part, Rüçhan Çıvgın, commercial director of Sanmar Shipyards, explained how the delivery “reflects both companies’ shared commitment to innovation, operational excellence and the development of sustainable towing solutions to meet the needs of modern ports.”

A Boğaçay class vessel based on Robert Allan’s RAmparts 2400SX-MKII design, the SAAM Hunabku stands out for its compact dimensions—24.4 meters in length and 12 meters in beam—combined with high operational capacity. It can reach speeds of up to 12.5 knots, is equipped with two CAT 3516E engines, has more than 80 metric tons of bollard pull, a FiFi-1 fire fighting system, dual azimuth propulsion (Z-drive), and can accommodate a crew of up to seven people.
